threat.name: Privilege escalation
threat.desc:
General Threat Description

Privilege escalation occurs when an entity gains elevated access to resources that are normally protected from an application or user. This can happen when a user or process gains rights or permissions beyond those originally granted, potentially leading to unauthorized system access or control.

Threat Agents/Attack Vectors

Attack vectors could include exploiting vulnerabilities in software, misconfigurations in security settings, or compromising lower-level user accounts that interact with Amazon ECS. This could be orchestrated by external attackers or malicious insiders.

Impacts

The impacts of privilege escalation are severe and can include unauthorized data access, data manipulation, and persistent access to the system, which might compromise the entire ECS cluster. It may also lead to further attacks on connected systems.

Example Attack Scenarios

An attacker might exploit a vulnerability in an application running in a container, allowing them to execute commands as a root user. Alternatively, an attacker could use a stolen set of credentials to modify ECS task definitions to run arbitrary commands, thereby escalating privileges within the cluster.

usecase.name: Denial of Service
usecase.desc: Denial of Service attacks aim to disrupt the availability of services or resources to legitimate users. Attackers overwhelm systems with excessive traffic or requests, causing them to become unresponsive or unavailable to users.

threat.name: Resource exhaustion
threat.desc:
General Threat Description

Resource exhaustion occurs when a system's resources, such as CPU, memory, or network bandwidth, are overwhelmed, typically by malicious intent. This can happen when excessive demands are placed on these resources, making the system slow or unresponsive.

Threat Agents/Attack Vectors

Attackers might employ scripts or bots to create a large number of tasks or services within Amazon ECS, or they might manipulate application processes to consume more resources than allocated. External attackers or malicious insiders could both exploit this vulnerability.

Impacts

Resource exhaustion can lead to denial of service (DoS), decreased application performance, and potential system crashes. In a cloud environment like ECS, it could also lead to increased costs due to resource scaling to meet the illegitimate demand.

Example Attack Scenarios

An attacker could deploy a container in ECS that purposely consumes an excessive amount of CPU and memory resources, affecting other containers running on the same cluster. Alternatively, an attacker could trigger a flood of requests that overwhelm the application, causing legitimate requests to time out or fail.

In order to establish secure communication between two parties, it is often important to adequately verify the identity of entities at each end of the communication channel. Inadequate or inconsistent verification may result in insufficient or incorrect identification of either communicating entity. This can have negative consequences such as misplaced trust in the entity at the other end of the channel. An attacker can leverage this by interposing between the communicating entities and masquerading as the original entity. In the absence of sufficient verification of identity, such an attacker can eavesdrop and potentially modify the communication between the original entities.

The use of weak, reused, and common passwords is rampant on the internet. Without the added protection of multiple authentication schemes, a single mistake can result in the compromise of an account. For this reason, if multiple schemes are possible and also easy to use, they should be implemented and required.

The end-to-end philosophy of checks states that integrity checks should be performed at the lowest level that they can be completely implemented. Excluding further sanity checks and input validation performed by applications, the protocol's checksum is the most important level of checksum, since it can be performed more completely than at any previous level and takes into account entire messages, as opposed to single packets.

countermeasure.name: Apply permission boundaries to cap Lambda role and user privileges
countermeasure.desc:
Define a single IAM permission-boundary policy that represents the maximum set of actions a Lambda workload should ever perform—typically the core lambda:*, CloudWatch Logs calls, and tightly scoped access to specific AWS resources. Attach that boundary to:

  • Every Lambda execution role (via the PermissionBoundary property in CloudFormation/Terraform).
  • All human or CI/CD principals that can create or update functions.

Because AWS evaluates the boundary before attached or inline policies, anything not explicitly allowed by the boundary is automatically denied—even if someone tries to grant broader rights later.

quick implementation

  1. Author and publish the boundary
    1. {
       "Version":"2012-10-17",
       "Statement":[
         { "Effect":"Allow", "Action":[
             "lambda:*",
             "logs:CreateLogGroup", "logs:CreateLogStream", "logs:PutLogEvents"
           ], "Resource":"*" },
         { "Effect":"Deny", "Action":[ "iam:*", "organizations:*", "lambda:DeleteFunction" ], "Resource":"*" }
       ]
      }
       
    2. aws iam create-policy --policy-name lambda-boundary --policy-document file://boundary.json
  2. Attach the boundary
    1. aws iam put-role-permissions-boundary \
          --role-name OrderProcessorRole \
          --permissions-boundary arn:aws:iam::<acct>:policy/lambda-boundary
  3. Enforce automatically
    • Add a pipeline check (e.g., cfn-lint, Checkov) that fails if a new role lacks PermissionBoundary.
    • Enable AWS Config rule iam-user-permissions-boundary-check and create a similar custom rule for roles to detect drift.
  4. Maintain
    Review the boundary every quarter: remove unused “Allow” actions, add new ones only after peer approval, and keep the policy version history in source control.

countermeasure.name: Deploy VPC Lambda functions across multiple Availability Zones
countermeasure.desc:
For every Lambda function that runs inside a VPC, attach at least two private subnets that reside in different Availability Zones (AZs). Lambda automatically spreads function instances across all subnets you specify, so providing subnets in multiple AZs gives the function resiliency against an AZ-level failure.

Implementation steps

  1. Subnet planning – In the target VPC, create two or more /24 (or smaller) private subnets, each located in a distinct AZ (for example, subnet-az1a-private, subnet-az1b-private). If the function needs outbound internet access, give every AZ its own NAT gateway or egress path.
  2. Configure the function
    • Console: Configuration → VPC ► Edit ► select the VPC and tick both (or all) private subnets.
    • AWS CLI / IaC:
      • aws lambda update-function-configuration \
         --function-name order-processor \
         --vpc-config SubnetIds=subnet-0a12…,subnet-0b34…,SecurityGroupIds=sg-0abc…
  3. Security groups – Attach a least-privilege security group that allows only the ports and CIDRs the function truly needs (for example, TCP 5432 to an RDS cluster SG).
  4. Guardrails – Implement an AWS Config custom rule or cfn-nag check that fails a deployment when a VPC-connected Lambda lists fewer than two subnets.
  5. Validation & monitoring – Use the Lambda console’s Monitoring → Subnet metrics or CloudWatch’s Duration metrics to confirm invocations appear from each AZ. Include a canary test that fires if an AZ’s invocations drop to zero.

Spreading subnets across Availability Zones ensures the function continues to invoke even if one AZ—or its networking components—becomes unavailable.

countermeasure.name: Encrypt Lambda env vars and code artifacts with customer-managed KMS keys
countermeasure.desc:
Safeguard every sensitive value that AWS Lambda stores—environment variables, .zip deployment packages, container images, and event-filter criteria—by encrypting them with an AWS KMS customer-managed key (CMK) instead of the default AWS-managed key. Using your own CMK lets you control key rotation, scope decrypt permissions tightly, and audit every use.

1 . Create or choose a CMK

aws kms create-key --description "Lambda data-at-rest CMK"
aws kms enable-key-rotation --key-id <key-id>

Limit the key policy to the Lambda service principal and the minimal set of roles that need kms:Decrypt / kms:GenerateDataKey.

2 . Encrypt environment variables

  • Console / IaC: set the KMS key ARN field (CloudFormation KmsKeyArn, Terraform kms_key_arn).
  • CLI:
    • aws lambda update-function-configuration \
          --function-name order-processor \
          --kms-key-arn arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789012:key/abcd…

Lambda now uses your CMK to encrypt Env Vars and event-filter JSON.

3 . Protect deployment artifacts

  • .zip packages in S3 – store them in a bucket with SSE-KMS and the same CMK:
    • aws s3api put-bucket-encryption \
          --bucket lambda-artifacts-prod \
          --server-side-encryption-configuration \
          '{"Rules":[{"ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault":
             {"SSEAlgorithm":"aws:kms","KMSMasterKeyID":"alias/lambda-data"}}]}'
  • Container images in ECR – ensure the ECR repository uses KMS encryption with your CMK.

4 . Grant least-privilege KMS access

Add this statement (scoped to the CMK ARN) to the function’s execution role:

{
 "Effect": "Allow",
 "Action": [
   "kms:Decrypt",
   "kms:GenerateDataKey*"
 ],
 "Resource": "arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789012:key/abcd…"
}

5 . Continuous assurance

  • Enable AWS Config rule lambda-function-env-vars-encrypted (or a custom rule) to flag functions without a CMK.
  • Create CloudWatch alarms on KMS metric NumberOfFailedDecryptRequests.
  • Rotate the CMK annually; update KmsKeyArn in templates, then disable the old key after confirming no decrypt errors.

Encrypting Lambda data with your own KMS keys gives you full custody of cryptographic material, meets stringent compliance mandates, and lets you trace every decrypt back to an invoking principal.

References

  • Encrypting environment variables and artifacts with a customer-managed KMS key
  • Using AWS KMS keys with AWS Lambda

countermeasure.name: Enforce bootstrap-aware CI/CD reviews and linting
countermeasure.desc:
To implement the security countermeasure that safeguards AWS Lambda custom runtimes by treating 'bootstrap' and Lambda runtime layers as sensitive code, follow the steps outlined below:

  1. Establish a Peer Review Process:
    • Define a policy that mandates peer reviews for any changes to files named 'bootstrap' or runtime layers containing 'bootstrap'.
    • Implement a system in your version control platform (e.g., GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket) that explicitly requires an "approval" label before merging code involving these sensitive components.
    • Ensure that reviewers are experienced in security practices and familiar with Lambda runtimes.
  2. Deploy Static Code Analysis Tools:
    • Integrate static analysis tools (e.g., Checkmarx, SonarQube) into the CI/CD pipeline.
    • Configure these tools to flag and fail builds when detected risky constructs such as:
      • curl, wget, or nc
      • Any usage of bash -c
      • Unchecked or blind network egress calls
    • Introduce an allowlist mechanism where risky constructs can only bypass checks if accompanied by a written, justified reason reviewed and approved by security teams.
  3. Restrict Bootstrap Role:
    • Verify that the 'bootstrap' file solely performs runtime initialization tasks and invokes the handler or Runtime Interface Client (RIC) as designed.
    • Apply rules to forbid any embedded persistence, telemetry beacons, or additional functionality within the 'bootstrap', unless explicitly approved through the peer-review process.
    • Audit the 'bootstrap' code periodically to ensure compliance with these restrictions.
  4. Enforce Pipeline-Only Deployment:
    • Block any direct uploads of Lambda runtime layers or the 'bootstrap' file via the AWS Management Console.
    • Configure permissions so that developers can only deploy changes through a CI/CD pipeline that enforces defined security checks.
    • Apply IAM policies to prevent unauthorized access to runtime layer modification workflows.

References

  • AWS Lambda Official Documentation
  • AWS CodePipeline Documentation
  • AWS Security Blog

countermeasure.name: Enforce code-signed Lambda deployments with AWS Signer
countermeasure.desc:
Guarantee that only vetted code reaches production by pairing AWS Signer with a Lambda Code Signing Configuration (CSC): every deployment package must be signed with your approved signing profile before Lambda accepts it.

  1. Create a signing profile
    1. aws signer put-signing-profile \
       --profile-name prod-lambda-code \
       --platform-id AWSLambda-SHA384-ECDSA
  2. Store the profile ARN in your CI/CD secrets.
  3. Integrate signing into the pipeline
    • Package the ZIP or container image, then call aws signer start-signing-job (ZIP) or ECR image signing (container).
    • Fail the build if the signing job status isn’t Succeeded.
  4. Define a Code Signing Configuration
    1. aws lambda create-code-signing-config \
       --allowed-publishers SigningProfileVersionArns=arn:aws:signer:…:profile/prod-lambda-code/* \
       --code-signing-policies UntrustedArtifactOnDeployment=Enforce
  5. Enforce blocks any unsigned or differently-signed artifact.
  6. Attach the CSC to functions
    1. aws lambda update-function-code-signing-config \
       --function-name orders-handler \
       --code-signing-config-arn arn:aws:lambda:…:code-signing-config:csc-abc123
  7. Include this step in all CloudFormation/Terraform modules so drift is impossible.
  8. Guardrails & monitoring
    • Enable the AWS Config rule lambda-function-code-signing-config-enabled to detect functions without a CSC.
    • Use EventBridge to alert when a deployment fails due to CodeSigningError, signalling a bypass attempt or pipeline mis-sign.
  9. Key hygiene
    • Rotate the Signer KMS key annually; update the signing profile to the new key version.
    • Restrict signer:StartSigningJob permission to the build role; deny it in production accounts via SCPs.

By requiring AWS-signed packages and enforcing CSCs, you shut the door on tampered artifacts, typo-squatted libraries, and shadow deployments.

References

  • Code signing for AWS Lambda
  • AWS Signer Developer Guide

countermeasure.name: Enforce tagging standards on Lambda functions
countermeasure.desc:
Every Lambda function must carry a complete, standardized tag set — for example Environment, Owner, CostCenter, and Compliance — so that security, cost-allocation, and automation workflows can rely on consistent metadata.

  5. Review quarterly
    • Spot-check tag accuracy (e.g., does the Owner tag still map to an active identity?) and update the standard when new reporting requirements appear.

Automated tagging enforcement guarantees that every Lambda function can be located, costed, and governed, while eliminating drift caused by manual provisioning.

countermeasure.name: Enforce TLS 1.2+ with perfect-forward-secrecy for all Lambda traffic
countermeasure.desc:
Ensure every network path that carries AWS Lambda control-plane or data-plane traffic—CLI / SDK calls to the Lambda API, Function URLs, ALB/API Gateway invokes, VPC egress, and third-party integrations—negotiates TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3 using PFS cipher suites (ECDHE or DHE). Disable legacy SSL/TLS versions and static-key ciphers to eliminate downgrade and session-key compromise risks.

Implementation guidance

  1. Runtime & library hardening
    • Use current AWS SDKs, AWS CLI v2, and OS packages (OpenSSL ≥ 1.1.1, Java ≥ 8 u181, .NET ≥ 4.6) that default to TLS 1.2+.
    • In container images or AMIs set MinProtocol = TLSv1.2 and remove *_RSA_* suites from the cipher list.
  2. Outbound Lambda networking
    • When the function runs in a VPC, allow only TCP 443 to interface endpoints (S3, STS, Secrets Manager, etc.). Block port 80 in security groups and route tables.
    • For external calls, pin the destination to https:// URIs and verify certificates (e.g., with Python requests.verify=True).
  3. Inbound invoke paths
    • Function URLs: set AuthType=AWS_IAM or another auth method; TLS is auto-enforced by AWS but add a WAF rule that blocks any request with the X-Forwarded-Proto != https.
    • API Gateway / ALB: enable TLS 1.2 minimum on the custom domain or listener policy; prefer ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-Res-2021-06.
    • For IoT or custom MQTT, use certificates that advertise only TLS 1.2/1.3 and EC cipher suites.
  4. Central guardrails
    • Attach an SCP that denies lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl or execute-api:Invoke when aws:SecureTransport is false.
    • Deploy AWS Config rules or cfn-nag checks that fail if an ALB listener policy includes TLS 1.0/1.1 or if a VPC security group permits port 80 egress.
  5. Continuous verification
    • Add a CI test that attempts openssl s_client -connect lambda.<region>.amazonaws.com:443 -tls1_1 and expect failure; succeed with -tls1_2.
    • Scan AMIs and containers monthly with Inspector or OpenSCAP for outdated OpenSSL/LibreSSL versions.
  6. Incident response & patching
    • Subscribe to AWS Security Bulletins; redeploy all Lambda runtime layers when critical TLS CVEs are announced.
    • Rotate any function URL or API Gateway custom certificates that use deprecated algorithms (RSA-1024, SHA-1).

Following this control guarantees strong, modern encryption end-to-end, satisfying compliance frameworks and protecting Lambda workloads against passive interception and forward-decryption attacks.

References

  • TLS 1.2 to become the minimum for all AWS service endpoints
  • Best practices for AWS Lambda security

countermeasure.name: Grant least-privilege IAM permissions to Lambda execution roles
countermeasure.desc:
Create a dedicated IAM role for every Lambda function and attach only the permissions the code truly needs—nothing more, nothing wildcard.

  1. Inventory required actions
    • List each AWS API the function calls (e.g., dynamodb:PutItem, s3:GetObject, secretsmanager:GetSecretValue).
    • Add logs:CreateLogGroup, logs:CreateLogStream, and logs:PutLogEvents for basic logging if they aren’t provided by a shared policy.
  2. Author a scoped policy
    • Restrict Resource to exact ARNs (specific table, bucket prefix, secret) instead of *.
    • Where possible, add condition keys—for example dynamodb:LeadingKeys, s3:prefix, aws:SourceVpc, or tag‐based conditions.
  3. Attach the policy to a unique execution role
    • Console: Configuration → Permissions → choose or create role.
    • IaC example (CloudFormation):
      • LambdaRole:
         Type: AWS::IAM::Role
         Properties:
           AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
             Statement:
               - Effect: Allow
                 Principal: Service: lambda.amazonaws.com
                 Action: sts:AssumeRole
           Policies:
             - PolicyName: OrdersFunctionPolicy
               PolicyDocument: {...}   # actions/resources from step 2
  4. Remove default privileges
    • Delete unused AWS-managed policies like AWSLambdaFullAccess.
    • Never attach AdministratorAccess or * actions—fail the pipeline if these appear.
  5. Continuous validation
    • Enable IAM Access Analyzer – unused permissions and prune actions that haven’t been called for 90 days.
    • Deploy AWS Config rule iam-managed-policy-check or a cfn-nag/Checkov rule in CI to block wildcard actions or resources.
  6. Review regularly
    • Re-run Access Analyzer after each feature release.
    • Rotate any secrets or keys the function accesses, updating the role policy as needed.

Applying strict, role-specific policies limits blast radius, supports the principle of least privilege, and satisfies compliance auditors looking for excessive permissions.

countermeasure.desc:
Run every Lambda function inside a dedicated set of private subnets and attach it to a least-privilege security group so the function can reach only the services it truly needs—nothing else.

How to implement

  1. Create “lambda-only” private subnets
    • Place them in the application VPC but do not route them to an Internet Gateway.
    • If outbound internet access is required, send traffic through a shared NAT Gateway or a VPC endpoint (for S3, DynamoDB, etc.).

    • Egress rules: allow only the ports and CIDRs (or other SGs) that correspond to your dependencies—for example, TCP 5432 to an RDS SG, HTTPS (443) to a Secrets Manager VPC endpoint SG. Remove the default “all traffic” egress rule.
    • Ingress rules: normally none are required; Lambda creates connections out of the subnet. If the function must be called by an internal ALB, allow only that ALB’s SG on the listener port.
  3. Attach the VPC config to the function
    1. aws lambda update-function-configuration \
       --function-name payment-handler \
       --vpc-config SubnetIds=subnet-0aa123,subnet-0bb456 \
                   SecurityGroupIds=sg-0lambda
  4. Guardrails and drift detection
    • Add an AWS Config rule (or cfn-nag/Checkov policy) that fails if a Lambda SG allows 0.0.0.0/0 or if the subnet route table points to an Internet Gateway.
    • Monitor VPC Flow Logs for unexpected destinations; tighten SG rules when new patterns appear.
  5. Document and review
    • Keep subnet IDs and SG IDs in your IaC modules so every environment uses the same isolation model.
    • Re-evaluate access rules quarterly or whenever the function’s dependencies change.

Locking Lambda functions into isolated subnets and SGs minimizes lateral movement, reduces the attack surface, and satisfies segmentation requirements without sacrificing performance.

AWS periodically deprecates Lambda runtimes (Node .js, Python, Java, .NET, Ruby, Go). A function that keeps running on an out-of-support runtime no longer receives security patches, and AWS may block deployments after the end-of-life date.

    • Use feature branches to bump the runtime version in your IaC (SAM/CloudFormation/Terraform) and CI pipeline, run tests, then deploy.
    • For container images, rebuild from an up-to-date base image and push a new tag.

    • Add a pipeline gate that rejects any create-function or update-function-configuration call if the --runtime flag is not in your approved list.
    • For containers, scan the image in CodeBuild/CodePipeline with AWS Inspector or Trivy before deployment.
  4. Review quarterly

Keeping all functions on supported runtimes guarantees ongoing security patches, performance optimisations, and access to the latest Lambda features.

countermeasure.name: Log all Lambda API activity with CloudTrail and secure S3 storage
countermeasure.desc:

  1. Enable a multi-Region trail
    • Console: CloudTrail → Trails → Create trail → select Apply trail to all Regions and log Management events – Read + Write (Lambda is covered automatically).

         --name org-lambda-trail \
         --s3-bucket-name org-trail-logs \
         --is-multi-region-trail

  2. Protect the S3 log bucket
    • Block public access and require TLS in the bucket policy:
      • "Condition": { "Bool": { "aws:SecureTransport": "false" } }
    • Enable SSE-KMS encryption with a customer-managed key; limit key-policy access to the CloudTrail service principal and your security team.
    • Turn on log file validation and bucket versioning to detect tampering.
  3. Retention & analytics
    • Apply lifecycle rules: e.g., keep logs in the S3 Standard tier for 90 days, then transition to Glacier Instant Retrieval or Deep Archive, deleting after seven years.
    • Optionally send the trail to CloudWatch Logs or Lake Formation for near-real-time detection and SQL-based hunting.
  4. Guardrails & monitoring
    • Deploy AWS Config rules such as cloudtrail-enabled and s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled so any drift triggers alerts.
    • Create EventBridge rules that notify your on-call channel when someone issues StopLogging, DeleteTrail, or changes the bucket policy.
  5. Periodic review
    • Quarterly, confirm that new AWS Regions and new Lambda features are still captured, and rotate or disable unused KMS keys and IAM principals.
    • Validate integrity with aws cloudtrail validate-logs during tabletop or incident-response exercises.

Implementing centralized, secure CloudTrail logging for Lambda provides an immutable audit trail that supports compliance, incident response, and continuous improvement of your serverless security posture.

countermeasure.name: Monitor package hash and bootstrap integrity
countermeasure.desc:
Implementing robust security countermeasures for AWS Lambda custom runtimes involves the following steps:

  1. Record Approved CodeSha256:
    • For every deployment of AWS Lambda, compute the CodeSha256 hash of the deployed function package using the AWS CLI or SDK.
    • Maintain an allowlist of approved CodeSha256 hashes in a secure system, such as AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store or a Configuration Management Database (CMDB) with audit logs enabled for modifications.
  2. Monitor Drift through EventBridge:
    • Create an EventBridge rule to capture UpdateFunctionCode events from CloudTrail. Configure CloudTrail to log all function updates to ensure full visibility of unplanned changes.
    • When an UpdateFunctionCode event is triggered, invoke a Lambda function or automation workflow that runs get-function against the affected Lambda function.
    • Compare the reported CodeSha256 from get-function output against the stored allowlist of approved hashes.
    • If a discrepancy is identified, create a high-severity finding and alert relevant teams immediately using an integrated mechanism such as AWS Security Hub or Amazon SNS.
  3. Verify Integrity During CI/CD:
    • In your CI/CD pipeline, compute and store a checksum for the bootstrap file (or its layer path) during the packaging step of Lambda custom runtimes.
    • For container-based runtimes, capture the digests of the container image and validate the ENTRYPOINT and CMD against the approved baselines stored during CI.
    • Post-deploy, verify the deployed checksums match the precomputed checksums from the CI/CD pipeline.
  4. Persist Integrity Metadata:
    • Store integrity metadata such as approved hashes, container digests, and runtime file checksums in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, with secure access controls to limit modifications to authorized personnel or automation scripts.
    • Enable versioning and tagging for stored metadata to support audit trails and provide recovery options in case of accidental modifications.
  5. Detect Unauthorized Bootstrap Changes:
    • Ensure that bootstrap file integrity validation is part of λ runtime monitoring. Regularly automate hash comparisons and include mechanisms for detecting tampering during runtime or in transit.
    • Integrate findings from the above monitoring mechanisms into AWS Security Hub or a centralized incident management tool for triage and resolution.

countermeasure.name: Require AWS_IAM authentication on Lambda function URLs
countermeasure.desc:
When you expose an AWS Lambda function through a Function URL, set the AuthType to AWS_IAM so that every invoke request must be SigV4-signed by an IAM principal with an explicit allow on lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl. This prevents unauthenticated internet traffic from reaching the function and lets you apply fine-grained least-privilege policies, MFA enforcement, and session-duration limits.

Implementation steps

  1. Create or update the Function URL
    1. aws lambda create-function-url-config \
         --function-name orders-handler \
         --auth-type AWS_IAM \
         --cors AllowedOrigins=https://app.example.com
      #—or—
      aws lambda update-function-url-config \
         --function-name orders-handler \
         --auth-type AWS_IAM
  2. Authorize callers
    • Add an IAM policy that allows lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl on the function ARN with /url suffix:
      arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789012:function:orders-handler:url
    • Scope the policy to trusted roles or users; require MFA or session tags if needed.
  3. Invoke securely
    • Clients must include an Authorization header with a SigV4 signature (aws4_request).
    • For browsers, front the URL with API Gateway or CloudFront signed cookies if you can’t sign requests client-side.
  4. Guardrails & monitoring
    • Deploy an AWS Config rule or SCP that prevents AuthType: NONE in production accounts.
    • Stream Lambda access logs to CloudWatch; alert on 403 errors to detect unauthorized attempts.

Using AWS_IAM authentication ensures only vetted principals can reach the function, leveraging the full power of IAM policies and audit trails.

countermeasure.name: Require MFA for root and IAM users
countermeasure.desc:
Protect the AWS account against credential theft by enforcing multi-factor authentication (MFA) on the root user and every IAM user:

  1. Enable MFA devices
    • Root user: sign in as root and register a hardware key, FIDO2 passkey, or virtual TOTP device at Account → Security credentials → Multi-factor authentication.
    • IAM users: in the IAM console or CLI (aws iam enable-mfa-device), attach a virtual or hardware MFA device to each user. Automate user creation so MFA is required before console access is granted.
  2. Block sessions without MFA
    • Attach an IAM policy that denies all actions when aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is false.
    • Apply an SCP at the OU or root level that prevents non-MFA console logins in production accounts.
  3. Monitor and enforce
    • Turn on AWS Config managed rules root-account-mfa-enabled and iam-user-mfa-enabled; alert when they report NON_COMPLIANT.
    • Stream CloudTrail to Security Hub and create findings if DeactivateMFADevice, DeleteVirtualMFADevice, or root logins without MFA occur.
  4. Operational hygiene
    • Register two MFA devices for the root user (primary and backup).
    • Review the IAM credential report monthly; disable or delete any user lacking MFA or with unused access keys.

Implementing mandatory MFA shuts down most credential-stuffing, phishing, and console-token replay attacks, forming the first and strongest line of defense for all Lambda-related and broader AWS operations.

countermeasure.name: Restrict lambda resource-based policies to explicit principals
countermeasure.desc:
Whenever you add a resource-based policy to a Lambda function (e.g., when granting another AWS account, an AWS service, or an API Gateway permission to invoke it), list only the exact IAM principal ARNs or service principals that require access.
Do not use wildcard principals ("*"), anonymous principals, or broad AWS service wildcards ("lambda.amazonaws.com" without conditions). Wildcards expose the function to unintended callers and defeat least-privilege design.

implementation checklist

  1. author precise statements
    1. {
       "Effect": "Allow",
       "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/PaymentService" },
       "Action": "lambda:InvokeFunction",
       "Resource": "arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:111122223333:function:ProcessPayment"
      }
  2. Specify the consuming account ID and role name; for cross-account access, pair with aws:SourceArn and aws:SourceAccount condition keys.
  3. block wildcards in CI/CD
    • Add cfn-nag / Checkov / cfn-guard rules that fail a build if Principal equals "*" or if no Condition keys are present for an AWS service principal.
  4. continuous compliance
    • Enable AWS Config rule lambda-function-public-access-prohibited (or a custom rule) to detect policies with public or wildcard principals and mark them NON_COMPLIANT.
    • Subscribe Security Hub to forward findings to your on-call channel so unintended permissions are fixed immediately.
  5. review quarterly
    • Use IAM Access Analyzer to enumerate current function resource policies and highlight new external principals.
    • Remove any stale or unused permissions.

Adhering to explicit-principal policies limits who can invoke or manage your Lambda functions, sharply reducing the risk of unauthorized access or privilege escalation.

countermeasure.name: Use PrivateLink interface endpoints for Lambda and supporting services
countermeasure.desc:
Create interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) for AWS Lambda and every service the function relies on—Lambda control plane (com.amazonaws.<region>.lambda), Function URLs (com.amazonaws.<region>.lambda-url), and supporting endpoints such as S3, ECR API/ECR DKR, CloudWatch Logs, KMS, DynamoDB, SQS, or Kinesis—so that all deployment, invoke, and dependency traffic stays on the AWS backbone instead of the public internet.

Implementation steps

  1. Subnet selection – choose at least two private subnets in different Availability Zones to give Lambda enough ENIs for scaling and AZ-level resilience.
  2. Provision endpoints – create each endpoint with the AWS CLI or IaC:
    1. aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint \
         --vpc-id vpc-1234abcd \
         --service-name com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.lambda \
         --vpc-endpoint-type Interface \
         --subnet-ids subnet-a subnet-b \
         --security-group-ids sg-lambda-endpoints
  3. keep Private DNS enabled so the standard service hostname automatically resolves to the VPC-local IPs.
  4. Harden network access – attach a security group that allows only TCP 443 from Lambda subnets or CI/CD hosts; block port 80 entirely.
  5. Apply endpoint policies – restrict calls to the exact actions your workload needs (e.g., lambda:InvokeFunction, lambda:GetLayerVersion) and, if required, add aws:SourceVpce or aws:SourceVpc conditions for defense-in-depth.
  6. Lock function resource policies – when using Function URLs or cross-account invokes, include StringEquals {"aws:SourceVpce":"vpce-…​"} so internet-sourced requests are rejected even if a public path exists.
  7. Validate – from a private instance run dig lambda.<region>.amazonaws.com and confirm it returns a 10.x address; disable the NAT Gateway temporarily and verify that deployments and invokes still succeed.
  8. Monitor and audit – enable VPC Flow Logs for the endpoint ENIs, set CloudWatch alarms on rejected flows, and add an AWS Config rule that flags production VPCs missing the Lambda endpoint.

PrivateLink keeps Lambda control-plane and data traffic inside AWS, reduces latency, simplifies firewall rules, and satisfies compliance mandates that prohibit internet egress for sensitive workloads.

  • AWS PrivateLink basics and best practices

countermeasure.name: Use temporary credentials via AWS STS
countermeasure.desc:
Give every Lambda function, service, CI/CD pipeline, and human operator an IAM role to assume rather than a static IAM user with access-key pairs. When a principal assumes the role, AWS Security Token Service (STS) hands back short-lived credentials (default ≤ 1 h) that AWS rotates automatically. This removes permanent secrets from code, cuts the blast radius of a leaked key, and lets you attach granular, least-privilege policies to each role.

Implementation steps

  1. Create purpose-built roles – one per Lambda function (execution role) and one per developer or automation persona. Scope policies to the minimum actions and resources needed.
  2. Configure assumption paths –
    • AWS services: add the service principal (e.g., lambda.amazonaws.com, codebuild.amazonaws.com) to the role’s trust policy so it can call sts:AssumeRole.
    • Humans/federation: use IAM Identity Center, SAML, or OIDC to let users assume their role after MFA.
  3. Remove static keys – disable or delete legacy IAM users and hard-coded keys; store only the role ARN in configuration.
  4. Set sensible session limits – keep MaxSessionDuration low (15 min–1 h for interactive work; ≤ 12 h for workloads).
  5. Monitor & audit – enable CloudTrail and IAM Access Analyzer to track who assumes which role; alert on unexpected roles or unusually long sessions.

Adopting STS-based roles wipes out long-lived credentials, enforces just-in-time access, and aligns with AWS recommended security posture.

Malicious alteration of Lambda function code or its dependencies—via compromised build pipelines, direct edits, or tainted layers—injects unauthorized logic into your serverless workloads.

  • Data exfiltration or tampering of event payloads and backend resources
  • Lateral movement via calls to other AWS services
  • Reputational harm and remediation costs

  1. CI/CD Injection: An attacker hijacks the build server to insert a reverse‑shell payload into the deployment ZIP.
  2. Console Swap: A compromised admin replaces production handler code via the AWS Console, embedding data‑exfiltration logic.

Custom runtimes in AWS Lambda rely on a 'bootstrap' file as their entry point, executed before reaching the handler. Without proper monitoring, this file can be manipulated to include malicious logic, enabling persistence across deployments.

The compromise of the 'bootstrap' file can lead to unauthorized data access, persistent backdoors in the runtime environment, and stealthy modifications that evade detection during typical security reviews.
Example Attack Scenarios
An attacker with deployment privileges embeds malicious code into the 'bootstrap' file that exfiltrates sensitive data to an external server. threat.name: Lack of audit logging
threat.desc:
General Threat Description
When Lambda API calls (e.g., CreateFunction, UpdateFunctionCode, InvokeFunction) aren’t captured by CloudTrail or centralized logging, unauthorized or malicious activity goes unrecorded.

Threat Agents / Attack Vectors

  • Malicious insiders or compromised roles making API calls
  • Automated tools invoking or updating functions without generating logs
  • Misconfigured CloudTrail trails or log‑delivery failures

Impacts

  • Undetected Changes: Function code or configuration modifications aren’t noticed
  • Forensic Blind Spots: Incidents can’t be reconstructed or attributed
  • Compliance Failures: Violation of audit‑logging mandates (e.g., PCI DSS, HIPAA)

Example Attack Scenarios

  1. An attacker updates a payment‑processing Lambda to include malicious logic; without CloudTrail logs, the change isn’t traced.
  2. A rogue script purges function versions via the SDK; absent audit entries, the deletions go unnoticed until failures occur.
  3. CloudTrail misconfiguration drops InvokeFunction records; a compromised role invokes backdoor functions repeatedly without alerting security teams.

threat.name: Lack of network isolation
threat.desc:
General Threat Description
When Lambda functions share flat or overly permissive network configurations—such as residing in default VPC subnets without segmentation or security‐group restrictions—they gain unfettered access to internal systems and the internet, increasing risk of lateral movement and data exfiltration.

Threat Agents / Attack Vectors

  • Threat Agents: Compromised function code, malicious insiders, or third‑party dependencies.
  • Attack Vectors:
    • Exploiting broad VPC subnet placement to reach databases, caches, or internal APIs.
    • Using SSRF or open‐redirect flaws within the function to pivot across network boundaries.
    • Leveraging unrestricted egress to exfiltrate data to attacker‑controlled endpoints.

Impacts

  • Lateral Movement: Attackers breach internal resources (e.g., RDS, Redis) via the compromised function’s network path.
  • Data Exfiltration: Sensitive payloads or environment variables are sent out over the internet.
  • Service Compromise: Unauthorized access to microservices, service meshes, or back‑end systems, undermining confidentiality and integrity.

Example Attack Scenarios

  1. Database Pivot: A stolen function token is used to invoke a Lambda in the default VPC, which then connects to an internal MySQL cluster on port 3306 to dump data.
  2. Internal Reconnaissance: An attacker injects SSRF payloads into a function endpoint, causing it to scan internal HTTP management interfaces and map out privileged services.
  3. Covert Exfiltration: A compromised dependency causes the function to upload decrypted S3 objects to an attacker’s external SFTP server, bypassing network ACLs.

threat.name: Lack of resource tagging
threat.desc:
General Threat Description
Without consistent tagging, Lambda functions can’t be programmatically identified for ownership, environment, or purpose—hindering cost tracking, security policy enforcement, and operational oversight.

Threat Agents / Attack Vectors

  • Agents: Negligent administrators, uncontrolled automation, and rogue deployments.
  • Vectors:
    • CI/CD pipelines creating functions without required Environment or Owner tags.
    • Manual console creations that omit security or compliance tags.
    • Third‑party tooling that doesn’t enforce tagging standards.

Impacts

  • Visibility Gaps: Security teams can’t quickly locate or audit sensitive functions.
  • Policy Evasion: Tag‑based IAM or GuardDuty suppression rules fail to apply, allowing unauthorized access.
  • Cost Overruns: Untracked “orphan” functions incur unexpected charges.
  • Cleanup Challenges: Hard to identify and decommission unused or outdated functions.

Example Attack Scenarios

  1. Hidden Malicious Function: An attacker deploys a backdoor Lambda without Team or Project tags—escaping routine audits and persisting undetected.
  2. Policy Bypass: A compromised automation role creates a function lacking the Compliance=PCI tag, sidestepping strict IAM permissions tied to that tag.
  3. Orphaned Resources: A deprecated service’s Lambdas remain untagged; months later, they still run and bill but aren’t owned or monitored by any team.

threat.name: Unauthorized invocation via public resource policies
threat.desc:
General Threat Description
Overly permissive Lambda resource policies (e.g. "Principal": "*") expose functions to anyone on the internet or any AWS account, allowing unauthorized parties to invoke them without credentials.

Threat Agents / Attack Vectors

  • Threat Agents: External attackers, malicious insiders, compromised third‑party accounts
  • Attack Vectors:
    • Resource‑based policies granting lambda:InvokeFunction to Principal: "*".
    • Cross‑account policies missing Condition: {"StringEquals": {"AWS:SourceAccount": ...}}.
    • Automated scanners discovering public ARNs and issuing invoke requests.

Impacts

  • Unauthenticated Execution: Attackers trigger functions at will, potentially running malicious logic.
  • Cost Overruns: High‑volume invocations rack up unexpected AWS charges.
  • Data Exposure & Tampering: Functions that read or write sensitive data can be abused to leak or corrupt information.
  • Downstream Disruption: Flooded event sources (queues, streams) or dependent services may be overwhelmed or fail.

Example Attack Scenarios

  1. Public Function Flood: An attacker discovers a public Lambda ARN and scripts thousands of InvokeFunction calls per minute, incurring heavy costs and throttling backend resources.
  2. Cross‑Account Abuse: A partner’s account has open invocation rights; a malicious actor uses it to invoke a payment‑processing Lambda with crafted payloads, creating fraudulent transactions.
  3. Data Leak via Unauthorized Payloads: A function tied to an S3 bucket runs on every invocation; by invoking it with custom payloads, an attacker tricks it into returning sensitive file contents in its response.

threat.name: Data interception in transit
threat.desc:
General Threat Description
Data interception in transit occurs when communication to or from Lambda functions—such as API Gateway requests, service‑to‑service calls, or event payloads—is sent without proper TLS or through misconfigured network paths, allowing adversaries to eavesdrop on or alter the data stream.

Threat Agents / Attack Vectors

  • Threat Agents: Network eavesdroppers, man‑in‑the‑middle attackers, malicious insiders
  • Attack Vectors:
    • Invoking Lambda over HTTP (API Gateway or Function URL) instead of HTTPS
    • Misconfigured VPC endpoints or transit gateways that don’t enforce encryption
    • Disabling or improperly validating TLS in SDKs or custom HTTP clients

Impacts

  • Credential Theft: API keys, JWTs, or signed URLs in request headers can be captured
  • Payload Exposure: Sensitive event data (PII, business logic) is readable in flight
  • Message Tampering: In‑transit modification of inputs or outputs leads to corrupted processing
  • Replay Attacks: Captured invocations can be resent to trigger unauthorized function executions

Example Attack Scenarios

  1. API Gateway Misuse: A function’s URL endpoint is configured for HTTP only. An attacker on the same network sniffs request bodies containing user credentials and session tokens.
  2. VPC Endpoint Bypass: Lambda communicates with an internal service through a VPC endpoint that doesn’t require TLS. A compromised EC2 instance in the VPC intercepts and logs unencrypted RPC calls.
  3. TLS Downgrade in SDK: A custom Python client disables certificate verification when calling a Lambda-backed API; an attacker performs a MITM attack to inject malicious payloads into the function’s execution.

threat.name: Data exposure at rest

General Threat Description
Data exposure at rest in AWS Lambda occurs when sensitive information—such as environment variables, function code packages, layers, or log snapshots—is stored unencrypted or with weak key management, making it accessible to unauthorized parties if storage systems are compromised.

Threat Agents / Attack Vectors

  • Threat Agents: Malicious insiders, compromised AWS credentials, and third‑party service breaches.
  • Attack Vectors:
    • Retrieving unencrypted Lambda environment variables or code bundles from S3/ECR.
    • Accessing /tmp storage on compromised execution hosts.
    • Downloading unencrypted CloudWatch log exports or Lambda layer artifacts.

Impacts

  • Secret Leakage: Exposed API keys, database passwords, or tokens.
  • Compliance Violations: Breach of at‑rest encryption mandates (PCI DSS, HIPAA, GDPR).
  • Lateral Movement: Harvested credentials enable access to other AWS resources.
  • Reputational & Financial Damage: Data breach remediation costs and loss of customer trust.

Example Attack Scenarios

  1. ECR Artifact Theft: An attacker with ECR read permissions pulls a Lambda image containing hard‑coded secrets in its code, extracting them offline.
  2. S3 Snapshot Breach: Misconfigured S3 bucket hosts unencrypted function packages; adversaries download and inspect code to harvest environment variables.
  3. Log Export Exposure: A support engineer exports CloudWatch logs (including sensitive payloads) to an unencrypted S3 bucket, which is later accessed by unauthorized users.

threat.name: Overly broad IAM permissions
threat.desc:
General Threat Description
Overly broad IAM permissions occur when AWS Lambda execution roles or associated policies grant more privileges than necessary—often using wildcards for actions or resources—exposing your functions to escalate privileges or access unrelated services.

Threat Agents / Attack Vectors

  • Threat Agents: Malicious insiders, compromised deployment pipelines, and external attackers using stolen credentials.
  • Attack Vectors:
    • IAM policies with "Action": "lambda:*" or "*" on "Resource": "*" attached to function roles.
    • Over‑permissive trust relationships allowing any principal to assume the Lambda role.
    • Failure to apply least‑privilege when granting access to AWS services (S3, DynamoDB, IAM).

Impacts

  • Privilege Escalation: Functions can call APIs beyond their scope (e.g., creating or deleting roles).
  • Data Breach: Exfiltration of sensitive data from S3 buckets, databases, or Secrets Manager.
  • Lateral Movement: Compromised functions pivot to other services or resources in your account.
  • Operational Disruption: Unintended changes to infrastructure, such as spinning up expensive resources or deleting critical stacks.

Example Attack Scenarios

  1. S3 Overreach: A Lambda role with s3:* on * is compromised; the attacker lists and downloads all buckets, harvesting PII.
  2. IAM Role Abuse: An overly broad iam:* permission lets a malicious function create a new admin user, granting full account control.
  3. Cost Shock: A function granted ec2:RunInstances and ec2:TerminateInstances is hijacked to spin up large fleets of instances, incurring massive charges and then deleting them to cover tracks.

threat.name: Outdated runtime environments
threat.desc:
General Threat Description
Outdated runtime environments occur when Lambda functions continue using deprecated or unpatched language runtimes (e.g. old Node.js, Python, Java versions), missing security fixes and performance improvements.

Threat Agents / Attack Vectors

  • Threat Agents: External attackers scanning for known CVEs, supply‑chain adversaries embedding exploits in dependencies.
  • Attack Vectors:
    • Exploiting publicly documented vulnerabilities in EOL runtimes.
    • Injecting malicious payloads through outdated library transitive dependencies.
    • Leveraging insecure default configurations tied to legacy runtimes.

Impacts

  • Remote Code Execution: Attackers exploit CVEs to run arbitrary code in your functions.
  • Data Breach: Compromised functions expose sensitive input or environment data.
  • Service Disruption: Unpatched bugs cause function crashes or performance failures.
  • Compliance Risks: Use of unsupported runtimes may violate organizational or regulatory policies.

Example Attack Scenarios

  1. CVE Exploit: A function running Python 2.7 is targeted with a known buffer‑overflow exploit, allowing an attacker to execute shell commands.
  2. Dependency Hijack: An outdated Node.js runtime pulls in a vulnerable version of a logging library; an attacker injects malicious code via crafted log messages.
  3. Misconfiguration Crash: A Java 8 function uses an old JDBC driver with memory‑leak bugs, causing repeated OOM errors and denial of service under load.

threat.name: Credential compromise
threat.desc:
General Threat Description
Credential compromise in AWS Lambda occurs when the secrets, API keys, or IAM credentials used by functions are exposed or stolen—either through code, environment variables, or execution context—allowing attackers to impersonate or control your serverless workloads.

Threat Agents / Attack Vectors

  • Threat Agents: Malicious insiders, automated bots, third‑party library leaks, compromised CI/CD pipelines
  • Attack Vectors:
    • Embedding secrets (AWS keys, database passwords) in function code or plaintext environment variables
    • Retrieving IAM role tokens from the Lambda execution environment via SSRF or metadata‑endpoint exploits
    • Exposing credentials in version control systems, build artifacts, or CloudWatch logs

Impacts

  • Unauthorized Function Invocation: Attackers invoke functions at will, potentially incurring costs or executing unwanted actions
  • Privilege Escalation & Lateral Movement: Stolen credentials grant access to other AWS services or higher‑privilege roles
  • Data Exfiltration & Tampering: Sensitive data processed by Lambdas (e.g., PII, business logic) can be read or modified
  • Service Disruption & Financial Loss: Illicit use of credentials can flood queues, trigger throttling, or bill for large-scale invocations

Example Attack Scenarios

  1. Hard‑coded Key Leak: A developer commits a Lambda function with embedded AWS keys to GitHub. An attacker clones the repo, uses the keys to read S3 buckets, and exfiltrates customer data.
  2. Metadata Endpoint Abuse: A malicious library loaded into the Lambda execution environment makes HTTP calls to the IMDS endpoint, harvesting the function’s IAM role token and using it to spin up new EC2 instances.
  3. Log Exposure: A misconfigured logging library prints database credentials from environment variables to CloudWatch Logs; a compromised IAM principal with logs:GetLogEvents reads the logs and uses the credentials to drop the database.

threat.name: Single‑AZ failure for VPC functions
threat.desc:
General Threat Description
When Lambda functions are placed in a VPC that spans only a single Availability Zone, an AZ outage (due to hardware failure, networking issues, or scheduled maintenance) renders those functions unable to access their ENIs, subnets, or dependent services—causing complete service disruption.

Threat Agents / Attack Vectors

  • AWS Infrastructure Failures: Power, network, or hardware faults isolated to one AZ.
  • Misconfiguration: VPC subnet or NAT gateway deployment limited to a single AZ.
  • Capacity Events: AZ‑specific resource exhaustion (e.g., ENI limits reached) preventing new function attachments.

Impacts

  • Service Outage: Affected Lambdas cannot execute, disrupting APIs, event processing, or back‑end jobs.
  • Data Delays: Queues and streams back up, leading to time‑sensitive data loss or processing lag.
  • Operational Costs: Emergency redeployments or cross‑AZ workarounds consume engineering time and may incur extra charges.

Example Attack Scenarios

  1. AZ Hardware Failure: A hardware fault knocks out networking in AZ A; all Lambda functions in that single‑AZ VPC lose ENI attachment and fail to process inbound events.
  2. NAT Gateway Capacity Spike: A DDoS flood targets the NAT gateway in the lone AZ, saturating its throughput; VPC‑bound Lambdas can’t reach the internet for API calls.
  3. Planned AZ Maintenance: AWS schedules maintenance that briefly disables ENI provisioning in AZ B; because all subnets reside there, no new Lambda invocations succeed until maintenance completes.

countermeasure.name: Enable automatic secret rotation in AWS Secrets Manager
countermeasure.desc:
To minimize the risk of unauthorized access due to stale or compromised secrets, configure AWS Secrets Manager to automatically rotate secrets at regular intervals. This ensures that secrets are periodically updated, reducing the likelihood of them being exploited by malicious actors. Follow these steps to implement automatic secret rotation:

Enable Secret Rotation:

  • Go to the AWS Secrets Manager console.
  • Select the secret you want to enable rotation for.
  • Click on "Rotate secret".

Define Rotation Schedule:

  • Choose a predefined schedule or specify a custom rotation interval (e.g., every 30 days). Use cron expressions for more granular control if needed.

Create a Lambda Function:

  • Develop an AWS Lambda function that handles the rotation logic. This function should:
    • Retrieve the current secret.
    • Generate a new version of the secret.
    • Update the secret in the relevant service or application.
    • Test the new secret to ensure it works correctly.
  • AWS provides sample Lambda functions for different use cases that can be customized to fit your requirements.

Attach the Lambda Function to the Secret:

  • In the rotation configuration, specify the ARN of the Lambda function that you created.
  • Configure the Lambda execution role with appropriate permissions to read and update the secret, as well as to update the application using the secret.

Test the Rotation Configuration:

  • Manually trigger a rotation to ensure that the Lambda function executes correctly and the secret updates without issues.
  • Monitor the logs and verify that the new secret is functioning as expected in the application.

countermeasure.name: Enforce TLS 1.2 or higher for AWS Secrets Manager communications

Verify TLS Configuration:

  • AWS Secrets Manager supports TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 by default for all API operations.

Update Client Applications:

  • Ensure that all client applications interacting with AWS Secrets Manager are updated to support TLS 1.2 or higher.
  • Update libraries and SDKs used by your applications to their latest versions, as they often include improved security features and support for modern TLS protocols.

Enforce TLS in Application Code:

  • Modify your application code to explicitly require TLS 1.2 or higher for connections to AWS Secrets Manager.
  • For example, in Python, use the botocore library which supports TLS 1.2 by default
  • In Java, ensure that the JVM is configured to use TLS 1.2 or higher:

Configure Network Settings:

  • Ensure that load balancers, proxies, and other network devices are configured to enforce TLS 1.2 or higher for inbound and outbound traffic.

Monitor and Audit:

  • Use AWS CloudTrail and AWS Config to monitor API calls and verify that all communications with AWS Secrets Manager are using the appropriate TLS version.
  • Set up CloudWatch Alarms to detect and alert on any communications that do not comply with the TLS 1.2 or higher requirement.

To ensure the privacy and security of traffic to AWS Secrets Manager, use private network routes such as AWS PrivateLink, VPN, or AWS Direct Connect. These methods help isolate traffic from the public internet, reducing the risk of interception and unauthorized access. Follow these steps to implement this control:

Set Up AWS PrivateLink:

    • Open the Amazon VPC console.
    • In the navigation pane, choose "Endpoints" and then "Create Endpoint."
    • Select "AWS Services" and choose "com.amazonaws.<region>.secretsmanager" from the service name list.
    • Select the VPC in which to create the endpoint.
    • Choose the subnets and security groups that will allow access to the endpoint.
  • Configure DNS:
    • Ensure that "Enable DNS name" is selected to allow private DNS resolution within your VPC.
  • Update Security Groups:
    • Modify the security groups associated with your resources to allow traffic from the VPC endpoint.

Set Up AWS Site-to-Site VPN:

  • Create a VPN Connection:
    • Open the Amazon VPC console.
    • In the navigation pane, choose "VPN Connections" and then "Create VPN Connection."
    • Configure the customer gateway and virtual private gateway settings.
    • Once the VPN connection is created, configure your on-premises router with the provided configuration details.
  • Establish the VPN Tunnel:
    • Ensure the VPN tunnels are up and that traffic is routing through the VPN connection.
  • Update Routing Tables:
    • Update the route tables in your VPC to direct traffic destined for AWS Secrets Manager through the VPN connection.

Set Up AWS Direct Connect:

  • Create a Direct Connect Connection:
    • Open the AWS Direct Connect console.
    • Choose "Create Connection" and select the appropriate location and port speed.
    • Once the connection is provisioned, set up the Direct Connect gateway and virtual interfaces (VIFs) to connect to your VPC.
  • Configure Network Routing:
    • Update your network routing to ensure that traffic to AWS Secrets Manager uses the Direct Connect path.

Configure Security Groups and Network ACLs:

countermeasure.name: Prevent logging of sensitive commands in command shells
countermeasure.desc:
To safeguard sensitive information from being inadvertently stored in command history logs, configure command shells and remote access programs to prevent the logging of commands that contain secret data. This practice helps in protecting secrets from unauthorized access. Follow these steps to implement this control:

Disable Command History Logging:

  • Bash: Add unset HISTFILE at the start of your session or include it in your .bashrc or .bash_profile file to prevent commands from being saved to history.
  • Zsh: Use unsetopt HIST_SAVE_NO_DUPS and set HISTSIZE=0 in your .zshrc to disable history logging.
  • Windows Command Prompt: Reduce the command history buffer size to 1.

Use Temporary Files for Secret Data:

  • Create a temporary file to store secret data
  • Restrict access to the file.
  • Write the secret to the file.
  • Immediately delete the file after use.

Clear Command History After Execution:

  • Bash: Clear history after executing sensitive commands

Configure Shell Profiles:

  • Bash: Set HISTSIZE=0 and HISTFILESIZE=0 in your .bashrc or .bash_profile to limit the size of the history file.
  • Zsh: Set HISTSIZE=0 and SAVEHIST=0 in your .zshrc to disable saving of command history.

Disable Logging in Remote Access Tools:

  • Ensure remote access programs (e.g., SSH) do not log command inputs containing sensitive information.
  • Review and adjust settings in tools like tmux and screen to avoid logging.

threat.name: Untracked user activities
threat.desc:
General Threat Description 

Untracked user activities refer to the lack of monitoring and logging of actions performed by users within AWS Secrets Manager. This absence of tracking can lead to undetected unauthorized access, changes, or misuse of secrets, compromising the security and integrity of the system. Without detailed logs, it is challenging to perform audits, identify security incidents, and attribute actions to specific users.

Threat Agents/Attack Vectors

  • External Attackers: Hackers gaining unauthorized access and performing actions without detection.
  • Insider Threats: Employees or contractors misusing their access without being tracked.
  • Misconfigured Systems: Systems lacking proper logging configurations, leading to unmonitored activities.
  • Automated Scripts: Scripts or bots performing actions that are not logged or monitored.

Impacts

  • Data Breach: Unauthorized access to and potential exfiltration of sensitive secrets.
  • Operational Disruption: Unmonitored changes leading to service disruptions or data integrity issues.
  • Financial Loss: Fraud or theft resulting from undetected malicious activities.
  • Reputation Damage: Loss of trust from customers and partners due to undetected and unaddressed security incidents.
  • Regulatory Non-Compliance: Failure to comply with data protection regulations requiring activity logging, resulting in legal and financial penalties.

Example Attack Scenarios

  1. Unauthorized Access: An attacker gains access to AWS Secrets Manager and retrieves sensitive secrets without being detected due to lack of logging.
  2. Insider Misuse: An employee with legitimate access modifies or deletes secrets, and the actions go untracked, preventing timely detection and response.
  3. Configuration Changes: Unauthorized configuration changes made by users are not logged, leading to potential security weaknesses that remain unnoticed.
  4. Malware Activity: Malware infects a system and performs unauthorized actions within AWS Secrets Manager, which are not tracked due to missing logs.

usecase.name: Information Disclosure
usecase.desc: Information disclosure occurs when sensitive data is exposed to unauthorized parties. This can include unauthorized access to confidential information, such as personal data, financial records, or intellectual property.

threat.name: Command history exposure
threat.desc:
General Threat Description 

Command History Exposure happens when sensitive information, like passwords or secret keys, is saved in the command history of a shell or CLI, potentially allowing unauthorized access.

Threat Agents/Attack Vectors

  • Internal Threats: Employees or contractors with CLI access.
  • External Attackers: Hackers or malware exploiting access.
  • Shared Systems: Multiple users with access to the same command history.

Impacts

  • Data Breach: Unauthorized access to sensitive secrets.
  • Financial Loss: Fraud or theft due to compromised secrets.
  • Operational Disruption: Service outages or data corruption.
  • Reputation Damage: Loss of customer trust.
  • Regulatory Non-Compliance: Legal and financial penalties.

Example Attack Scenarios

  1. Shared Workstation: Another user accesses command history to find secrets.
  2. Compromised Account: Phishing attack reveals command history with secrets.
  3. Insecure Remote Access: Attacker intercepts session, accesses command history.
  4. Insider Threat: Employee uses command history to disrupt operations.

threat.name: Static secrets
threat.desc:
General Threat Description 

Static secrets refer to credentials, passwords, or other sensitive data that remain unchanged over extended periods. When secrets are not rotated regularly, they become vulnerable to unauthorized access if they are leaked or discovered. Static secrets can be compromised through various means, including social engineering, brute force attacks, or insider threats.

Threat Agents/Attack Vectors

  • External Attackers: Hackers using stolen or leaked credentials to access sensitive information.
  • Insider Threats: Employees or contractors with access to static secrets misusing their access.
  • Social Engineering: Attackers tricking individuals into revealing static secrets.
  • Brute Force Attacks: Repeated attempts to guess static passwords or credentials.

Impacts

  • Data Breach: Unauthorized access to sensitive information, leading to data leakage.
  • Operational Disruption: Compromised secrets can result in service outages or unauthorized changes to systems.
  • Financial Loss: Theft or fraud resulting from the misuse of static secrets.
  • Reputation Damage: Erosion of trust and credibility with customers and partners due to security breaches.
  • Regulatory Non-Compliance: Legal and financial penalties due to failing to meet data protection standards.

Example Attack Scenarios

  1. Leaked Credentials: An attacker obtains static credentials from a leaked database and uses them to access AWS Secrets Manager, extracting sensitive secrets.
  2. Insider Misuse: An employee with knowledge of static secrets leaves the company but continues to use the credentials to access sensitive systems and data.
  3. Phishing Attack: An attacker successfully phishes an employee, gaining access to static secrets that have not been rotated in months.
  4. Brute Force Attack: An attacker uses automated tools to repeatedly attempt to guess static passwords until they gain access to sensitive accounts.

By regularly rotating secrets and implementing automated secret management practices, organizations can significantly reduce the risk associated with static secrets.

threat.name: Inter-network traffic exposure
threat.desc:
General Threat Description 

Inter-Network Traffic Exposure occurs when data transmitted between AWS Secrets Manager and other systems is not adequately protected, allowing unauthorized entities to intercept, modify, or steal sensitive information. This threat arises from the use of unsecured or improperly configured network connections.

Threat Agents/Attack Vectors

  • External Attackers: Hackers intercepting unencrypted data transmissions over the internet or other networks.
  • Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) Attacks: Attackers intercepting and potentially altering data between AWS Secrets Manager and its clients.
  • Improper Configuration: Misconfigured network settings or lack of encryption leading to exposure of sensitive traffic.

Impacts

  • Data Breach: Unauthorized access to sensitive secrets during transmission.
  • Data Integrity Compromise: Modification of data during transmission, leading to corrupted or malicious data.
  • Operational Disruption: Interruption of services due to compromised data integrity or availability.
  • Reputation Damage: Loss of trust from customers and partners due to exposure of sensitive data.
  • Regulatory Non-Compliance: Violations of data protection regulations, resulting in fines and legal actions.

Example Attack Scenarios

  1. Unencrypted API Calls: An attacker intercepts unencrypted API calls between a client application and AWS Secrets Manager, gaining access to sensitive secrets.
  2. MitM Attack: An attacker positions themselves between a client and AWS Secrets Manager, capturing and possibly altering data in transit.
  3. Improper VPN Configuration: A misconfigured VPN connection exposes traffic to interception by unauthorized parties.

threat.name: Improper encryption key management
threat.desc:
General Threat Description 

Improper Encryption Key Management involves weaknesses in the creation, storage, distribution, rotation, and destruction of encryption keys used to protect secrets in AWS Secrets Manager. Inadequate management of encryption keys can lead to unauthorized access, data breaches, and compromised data integrity.

Threat Agents/Attack Vectors

  • Internal Threats: Employees or contractors mishandling encryption keys.
  • External Attackers: Hackers exploiting weak key management practices.
  • Insider Threats: Malicious insiders misusing encryption keys.
  • Misconfigured Systems: Improperly configured key policies or permissions.

Impacts

  • Data Breach: Unauthorized access to encrypted secrets.
  • Data Integrity Compromise: Corrupted or tampered data.
  • Financial Loss: Fraud or theft due to exposed secrets.
  • Operational Disruption: Service outages and loss of data availability.
  • Regulatory Non-Compliance: Legal and financial penalties due to non-compliance.

Example Attack Scenarios

  1. Weak Key Policies: An attacker exploits a weakly configured key policy to decrypt secrets.
  2. Unrotated Keys: Stale encryption keys are compromised, giving an attacker access to encrypted data.
  3. Excessive Permissions: An insider with unnecessary permissions accesses and misuses encryption keys.
  4. Misconfigured KMS: Misconfiguration in AWS KMS allows unauthorized users to generate or access keys.

threat.name: Unencrypted data transmission
threat.desc:
General Threat Description 

Unencrypted data transmission refers to the risk associated with transmitting sensitive information, such as secrets and credentials, over a network without encryption. This lack of encryption can lead to unauthorized interception, eavesdropping, and manipulation of data during transit, compromising the confidentiality and integrity of the information.

Threat Agents/Attack Vectors

  • External Attackers: Hackers intercepting unencrypted data packets traveling over public or internal networks.
  • Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) Attacks: Attackers positioning themselves between the sender and receiver to capture or alter data.
  • Insider Threats: Employees or contractors with access to network traffic capturing unencrypted transmissions.
  • Network Sniffing Tools: Use of tools to monitor and capture unencrypted data packets on the network.

Impacts

  • Data Breach: Exposure of sensitive secrets and credentials, leading to unauthorized access.
  • Data Integrity Compromise: Alteration of data during transmission, resulting in corrupted or malicious information.
  • Operational Disruption: Interference with data transmission causing service outages or degraded performance.
  • Financial Loss: Fraud or theft due to intercepted and misused secrets.
  • Reputation Damage: Loss of trust from customers and partners due to compromised data security.
  • Regulatory Non-Compliance: Failure to comply with data protection regulations, resulting in legal and financial penalties.

Example Attack Scenarios

  1. Intercepted API Calls: An attacker intercepts unencrypted API calls between a client application and AWS Secrets Manager, gaining access to sensitive secrets transmitted in plain text.
  2. MitM Attack on Public Network: An attacker on a public Wi-Fi network captures unencrypted data packets containing credentials and uses them to access sensitive resources.
  3. Internal Network Sniffing: An insider uses network sniffing tools to capture unencrypted secrets transmitted between internal systems, leading to unauthorized access.
  4. Compromised VPN Connection: A VPN connection without proper encryption is compromised, allowing an attacker to intercept sensitive data transmitted between on-premises networks and AWS Secrets Manager.

threat.name: Undetected anomalous activities
threat.desc:
General Threat Description 

Undetected anomalous activities refer to unusual or suspicious actions within AWS Secrets Manager that go unnoticed due to a lack of monitoring and alerting mechanisms. These activities could indicate potential security incidents, such as unauthorized access, malicious usage, or configuration changes, which, if not detected promptly, can lead to significant security breaches and data loss.

Threat Agents/Attack Vectors

  • External Attackers: Hackers exploiting vulnerabilities or using stolen credentials to perform unauthorized actions.
  • Insider Threats: Employees or contractors misusing their access to perform malicious activities.
  • Automated Bots: Malicious bots performing repetitive actions that deviate from normal usage patterns.
  • Misconfigured Systems: Systems or applications unintentionally performing unexpected actions due to misconfigurations.

Impacts

  • Data Breach: Unauthorized access to and potential exfiltration of sensitive secrets.
  • Operational Disruption: Unnoticed changes or deletions of secrets leading to service outages or degraded performance.
  • Financial Loss: Fraud or theft resulting from undetected malicious activities.
  • Reputation Damage: Loss of customer trust and business credibility due to delayed incident response.
  • Regulatory Non-Compliance: Failure to detect and report security incidents may result in legal and financial penalties.

Example Attack Scenarios

  1. Credential Stuffing: An attacker uses a list of stolen credentials to access AWS Secrets Manager. Without monitoring, these repeated access attempts go unnoticed, leading to a breach.
  2. Insider Data Exfiltration: An employee with legitimate access slowly exfiltrates sensitive data over time. The lack of anomaly detection prevents timely discovery of the breach.
  3. Configuration Changes: An unauthorized user changes the configuration of secrets or permissions, disrupting services. Without alerts, the changes remain undetected until services are impacted.
  4. Malware Activity: Malware infects a system with access to AWS Secrets Manager and performs unauthorized activities. The lack of anomaly detection allows the malware to operate undetected for an extended period.

threat.name: Inadequate network access controls
threat.desc:
General Threat Description 

Inadequate Network Access Controls refer to the failure to properly restrict and secure network access to AWS Secrets Manager. This can result in unauthorized entities gaining access to sensitive secrets, leading to potential data breaches and exploitation of critical information.

Threat Agents/Attack Vectors

  • External Attackers: Hackers exploiting weak network security configurations to access AWS Secrets Manager.
  • Insider Threats: Employees or contractors with excessive network permissions accessing secrets without proper authorization.
  • Misconfigured Network Settings: Incorrectly configured security groups, network ACLs, or VPC endpoints allowing unintended access.

Impacts

  • Data Breach: Unauthorized access to sensitive secrets.
  • Financial Loss: Fraud or theft due to exposed secrets.
  • Operational Disruption: Service outages or corrupted data.
  • Reputation Damage: Loss of customer trust and business credibility.
  • Regulatory Non-Compliance: Legal and financial penalties due to non-compliance with data protection laws.

Example Attack Scenarios

  1. Open Security Groups: Security groups are configured to allow access from any IP address, enabling attackers to connect to AWS Secrets Manager and retrieve secrets.
  2. Misconfigured VPC Endpoints: VPC endpoints are not restricted to specific subnets, allowing broader network access than intended.
  3. Insider Abuse: An employee with network access permissions abuses their access to retrieve and misuse secrets from AWS Secrets Manager.
  4. Unsecured Network ACLs: Network ACLs are not properly configured, allowing unauthorized inbound and outbound traffic to access secrets.

countermeasure.name: Apply authorization checks to segregate and control access to user data
countermeasure.desc:
Applications protecting sensitive or otherwise restricted resources must ensure that only appropriate and authorized users can access the application data. It is important that an application prevent unauthorized users gaining inappropriate access to each other's data. Although user A and user B may both be trusted to access data within the application, they may be only authorized to access different subsets of the protected resources.  E.g. user A should not be able to access user B's personal data by manipulating a request (typical examples are the manipulation of an ID value or other object reference sent in the URL or body of an HTTP request).

It is not sufficient to rely on obscurity, for example obfuscated or secret URLs or filenames. The application must validate each request for protected data against the proven identity of the user. Before providing access to restricted resources the application must:

  • Ensure the user has undergone appropriate authentication (identification and verification, or ID&V). E.g. they must have provided their identity and confirmed this with a password, token, or other verification. Typically this is done by checking the validity of the session token issued after login.
  • Confirm the user is authorized to access the data or resource they are requesting. E.g. their confirmed identify is checked against a server-side access control matrix to determine whether they may access the requested resource.
  • Access controls should be granular and make it possible to issue to individual resources to individual users or roles.

URL and asset based access control is provided by most web-frameworks, and it is preferable to use an established and proven framework.

Object-level authorization checks should be considered in every function that accesses a data source using input from the user.

Remediation:

  • Favor not using an ID that has been sent from the client, but instead use an ID that is stored in the session object when accessing a database record by the record ID.
  • Use an authorization mechanism to check if the logged-in user has access to perform the requested action on the record in every function that uses an input from the client to access a record in the database.
  • Use random and unpredictable values as GUIDs for records' IDs.
  • Write tests to evaluate the authorization mechanism. Do not deploy vulnerable changes that break these tests.
